outline.chapter_title: Chapter 1: Case Background and Procedural Posture
outline.description: This chapter establishes the factual context of the dispute involving GoAuto Insurance and its financing partner, APAC. It details the mechanism by which insureds finance their premiums, the specific events leading to policy cancellations due to non-payment, and the subsequent litigation history. The chapter traces the path from the initial state court filing to removal to federal court, explaining why the case proceeded as a motion for summary judgment focused exclusively on statutory compliance rather than broader bad faith claims.
subtopics: The relationship between insureds, GoAuto Insurance, and American Premium Assistance Company (APAC)
The role of Power of Attorney in premium finance agreements
The sequence of non-payment and automated cancellation triggers
Procedural history: State court filing, removal to Federal District Court, and motions for summary judgment
The scope of review: Why the appeal focuses solely on statutory compliance regarding cancellation procedures

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 2: Governing Legal Standards under Louisiana Law
outline.description: Before analyzing GoAuto's conduct, this chapter outlines the specific statutory framework governing insurance cancellations in Louisiana. It explains La. Rev. Stat. § 9:3550(G)(3), detailing the four mandatory certifications required from a premium finance company. Crucially, it introduces the doctrine of 'strict adherence,' citing key Louisiana precedents that establish any defect in this process renders a cancellation void ab initio. This sets the high bar that plaintiffs argue GoAuto failed to meet.
subtopics: Statutory text of La. Rev. Stat. § 9:3550(G)(3)(a)(i)-(iv)
The four mandatory components of a valid cancellation notice
The doctrine of strict adherence in Louisiana insurance law
- Purpose 1: Fixing the exact time/date of cancellation
- Purpose 2: Providing a cure period for defaults
Key precedent establishing that defects invalidate cancellations (*Delatte*, *Eaglin*, *Britten*)

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 3: Analysis of Signature Requirements and Corporate Certification
outline.description: This chapter examines the first major legal issue: whether the statute requires a handwritten or digital signature from a named employee on the certification notice before a policy can be cancelled. The court analyzes GoAuto's procedure—where an email is generated automatically at midnight followed by a signature stamp applied later—and contrasts it with plaintiffs' interpretation. The court reviews existing Louisiana case law (or lack thereof) regarding signatures and concludes that corporate certification does not mandate an individual's signature if other statutory elements are met.
subtopics: 'Strict adherence' vs. adding procedural hurdles not found in statutory text
'Certifying' versus 'signing': Analyzing semantic requirements
'Reviewing relevant case law (*Benitez*, *KMJ Servs.*, *Hodges*) regarding identification requirements'
- Distinguishing cases where lack of ID was fatal vs. cases where it was not
- Conclusion that corporate certification suffices without individual identification or pre-cancellation signatures

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 4: Defining 'Receipt' in an Automated Digital Environment
outline.description: This chapter addresses the second critical issue: whether GoAuto obtained 'receipt' of the cancellation request prior to cancelling the policy when its computer system acted automatically based on an incoming email from APAC's system before any human interaction occurred.The court interprets'death'in lightof modern technology,discussing how'delivery'to a computer system constitutes'receipt'.It rejectsplaintiffs'argumentthatphysicalpossessionbyahumanemployeeisrequiredandaffirmsthatthedigitalhandshakebetweenweb services satisfies statutory mandates.
